phonemes.desc: Short iota with smooth breathing — the name opens light and quick, without roughness.
Long alpha with acute pitch [áː] — the stressed peak of the name; the Ionic form Ἰήσων, with long eta, proves the vowel's length.
Sigma followed by long omega [sɔːn] — the drawn-out final syllable that marks the name as long-voweled.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ih-AH-sone' — the second syllable is pitched higher and held; the final 'ō' is long and closed, nothing like the English 'sun'.

kin.label: Greek verb
kin.form: ἰάομαι, 'to heal, to cure' — the root of the name

kin.label: Greek noun
kin.form: ἰατρός, 'physician', built on the same root

kin.label: Ionic Greek
kin.form: Ἰήσων (Iḗsōn), the Ionic form with long eta standing for Attic long alpha

pronunciation.note: Iásōn is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἰάσων contains both stress (acute on the long alpha) and length (the long ᾱ and the final ω). The restoration keeps both: the acute on á and the macron on ō. The name means 'healer' — a fact the quest story tends to forget.

domains.title: The Healer Who Sailed
domains.subtitle: Heroism, the Golden Fleece, and the First Great Voyage
domains.lead: Iásōn is the captain of the first great sea-quest of Greek myth: the voyage of the Argo to Colchis for the Golden Fleece. His name comes from ἰάομαι, 'to heal' — yet his story is less about curing than about gathering: he is the hero whose greatest power is to summon other heroes, and to win the love of a princess whose magic does the work.

cards.name: The Argo
cards.desc: The first true ship, built by Argos the shipwright under Athena's direction; its prow held a beam from the speaking oak of Dodona.

cards.name: The Golden Fleece
cards.desc: The fleece of the flying ram that carried Phrixos to Colchis, hung in a grove of Árēs and guarded by a sleepless dragon.

cards.name: The Argonauts
cards.desc: Some fifty heroes — Heraklēs, Orpheus, the Dioskouroi, Atalanta in some tellings — the greatest muster before Troy.

cards.name: The Healer's Name
cards.desc: From ἰάομαι, 'to heal' — the ironic name of a hero whose cures are worked by Medea's pharmaka, not his own hands.

symbols.name: Golden Fleece
symbols.meaning: The object of the quest, token of the kingship to be restored

symbols.name: The Argo
symbols.meaning: The first ship; its name, 'swift', shares the shining root ἀργός

symbols.name: The single sandal
symbols.meaning: The sign of the oracle — the one-sandaled man who would undo Pelias

symbols.name: Dragon's teeth
symbols.meaning: Sown in Colchis, they sprouted armed men — the trial Aietēs set him

symbols.name: The dove
symbols.meaning: Loosed at the Clashing Rocks on Phineus's counsel; its safe passage showed the way

mythology.lead: The myth of Iásōn is the myth of the quest itself: an unjust king, an impossible errand, a band of heroes, and a prize won by cunning and love rather than by strength alone. Pindar sang it; Apollonius made it an epic; Euripides gave it its dark ending.

myths.title: The Man with One Sandal
myths.text: Pelias, who had seized the throne of Iolkos from Iásōn's father Aisōn, was warned by an oracle to beware the man wearing one sandal. Iásōn came down from Mount Pelion, where the centaur Cheirōn had reared him, and lost a sandal fording the river Anauros — carrying, Apollodorus says, an old woman who was Hera in disguise. Pelias saw the sign and set the errand he thought would kill him: fetch the Golden Fleece from the edge of the world.

myths.title: The Argo and the Clashing Rocks
myths.text: The greatest heroes of the age answered the summons. The Argo sailed from Pagasai through wonders and losses — Lemnos, the land of women; the death of Hylas, which cost them Heraklēs; the boxing of Polydeukēs with Amykos — until Phineus, the blind seer, told them how to pass the Symplegades, the rocks that clashed together. A dove was loosed first; when it lost only its tail-feathers, the Argonauts rowed through on the rebound, and the rocks stood still forever.

myths.title: Medea and the Tasks of Aietēs
myths.text: In Colchis, King Aietēs set three labors: yoke the fire-breathing bulls, plow the field of Árēs, and slay the armed men sprung from a dragon's teeth. Hera and Athena persuaded Aphrodite to send Eros, and Medea, the king's daughter and a priestess of Hekate, fell in love with the stranger. Her ointment made Iásōn proof against fire and iron for a day; her counsel felled the dragon's brood; her charm sang the sleepless guardian to sleep, and the Fleece was taken in the night.

myths.title: The Betrayal at Corinth
myths.text: The homecoming was shadowed from the start: in Apollodorus's telling Medea had dismembered her brother Apsyrtos to slow the pursuit, and at Iolkos she tricked Pelias's daughters into cutting their father to pieces in a false rite of renewal. Exiled to Corinth, Iásōn put Medea aside to marry the princess Glaukē. Euripides tells the rest — the poisoned robe, the murdered children, the chariot of the Sun. Iásōn died as he had lived, by the Argo: struck in old age by a beam of the rotting ship as he slept beneath it.

lore.syncretism: A mortal hero drew no foreign cult identifications of the sort the Olympians attracted; Iásōn's syncretism is literary and linguistic. Rome made him Iāsōn in epic (Valerius Flaccus) and elegy (Ovid's Heroides), and through Latin his name passed into every European language. More strikingly, Hellenistic Jews adopted Ἰάσων as the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew Yehōšūaʿ (Joshua): a Jason appears among the high priests of Jerusalem in the books of Maccabees, and a Jason of Thessalonica shelters Paul in the Acts of the Apostles. The healer's name, born in Thessaly, ended as one of the bridge-names between the Greek and Hebrew worlds.
lore.culturalLegacy: Iásōn founded a genre: every quest narrative, from the medieval grail romances to the modern space voyage, retraces the Argo's wake. The very word 'argonaut' became the common noun for the far-sailing adventurer — and, by derivation, 'astronaut' and 'aquanaut'. William Morris retold the whole myth in The Life and Death of Jason (1867); Ray Harryhausen's film Jason and the Argonauts (1963) fixed the image for a century of cinema. As a given name, Jason ranked among the most popular in the English-speaking world of the late twentieth century. The restoration Iásōn returns to the familiar name its forgotten meaning: the healer who sailed.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Iásōn is the strangest of the great Greek heroes, because he is the least heroic by the usual measures. He slays no monster unaided; the fire-breathing bulls are mastered through an ointment, the dragon through a lullaby, the Fleece itself through a princess's love. His one distinctive gift is the gift of gathering — the summons that brought fifty heroes to one beach, and the charm that won Medea. The Greeks half-noticed this: Pindar treats him as the gentle answer to his homeland's sickness, and the tragedians show a man perpetually outmatched by the powers he sets in motion.

That is why his ending is so quietly terrible. There is no grand hubris, no defiance of the gods — only drift. He owes everything to a woman and trades her for a useful marriage, and the universe answers in kind. The man named 'healer' leaves behind him a trail of the cut and the broken: Apsyrtos, Pelias, his own children. Perhaps that is the lesson the myth keeps: a name is a task, not a possession. Iásōn never healed anyone. The name waited, and in another tongue, on another shore, it was carried by healers again.
lore.archaeology: Iolkos, the city Iásōn was born to rule, lies beside modern Volos: Mycenaean remains at Dimini and at the palace-site of ancient Iolkos keep the legend anchored, and the bay of Pagasai, the Argo's port, is the bay of Volos itself. Across the Black Sea, Colchis is historical Georgia, where the site of Vani has yielded astonishing gold-work of the fifth–fourth centuries BCE; the geographer Strabo reports that Colchian miners washed gold from mountain streams with fleeces — the rationalist's explanation for the Fleece. No temple or cult of Iásōn is securely attested; his monument was a story.
